why: Evidence: zero errors everywhere - canary 0 5xx / 0.00% err over 2476 requests, same as stable (7343 reqs, 0 5xx). The only negative signal is latency in the aggregate: canary p95 177ms vs stable 94ms, p99 218 vs 104, and every route slower (/browse 150 vs 27, /search 177 vs 59, /checkout 215 vs 103). But the over-time table shows that gap is entirely front-loaded: canary p95 by window is 210 -> 130 -> 95 -> 94 while stable holds flat at 93/94/95/94. By the 60-90s window the canary matches stable, and in 90-120s it is identical (94 vs 94). Judgement: this decaying-then-converging shape is a warmup artifact (cold JIT / empty caches / cold connection pools on a pod that has just started), not a steady-state regression - a real code or query regression would stay elevated or grow for the full 120s rather than settling exactly onto the stable baseline. The aggregate p95 is therefore dominated by the first ~30-60s of a 120s test and overstates the steady-state cost. With steady-state latency at parity and no error-rate signal, the customer risk of promoting is low. Caveats I am accepting as risk: only 1 canary pod and ~2.5k requests, so this is a single warmup observation; the last two windows are 30s each, so the at-parity evidence is roughly 60s long. Follow-up: after promote, watch p95 during the rollout as each new pod warms (expect a transient bump per pod, matching the 0-30s pattern), keep the rollout surged/gradual with readiness gates so cold pods do not take full traffic, and roll back if p95 stays above ~110ms for more than 2 minutes after the last pod is ready or if any 5xx appear.
